## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mittāmittajātaka* (Ja 197) is a birth story preserved in the Pali *Jātaka* collection, translated under the title *Friends and Enemies*. The narrative opening relates that the Buddha delivered the teaching while residing at Sāvatthi, occasioned by a monk who took a piece of cloth from his preceptor out of personal trust (*vissāsena*) to fashion a shoe-bag [Fausböll 1879]. The canonical verse opening begins with the words *Na naṁ umhayate disvā* ("He smiles not on seeing him") [Fausböll 1879].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta elucidates the distinguishing signs of friends and foes (*mittāmittabhāvakāraṇāni*), develops the *brahmavihāra*s, and is reborn in the Brahmā world [Fausböll 1879]. Concluding the narrative (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the past characters: an elephant-rearing ascetic was the co-resident monk, the elephant was his preceptor, the gathering of sages was the Buddha's following, and the leader of the company was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1879].

 This textual relationship is corroborated by DharmaNexus, which detects six matching Pali-internal reuse passages (totaling 398 characters; longest alignment §1.1–1.4 with §1791–1792 at a similarity score of 0.96) between this text and the fourth volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, where Ja 473 is situated [DharmaNexus].
